title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation from natural‑language operator intent to concrete device configuration is an active NetOps research direction with potential operational benefits. However, prior work shows LLMs can produce a range of mechanically detectable faults—syntax mistakes, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy errors—that, if applied in production, could cause outages or unintended access [1], [4]. A common mitigation pattern is to pair a generator with a deterministic verifier and, where the verifier reports violations, invoke limited model‑guided repair; we call this generate–verify–repair (GVR). Prototype studies across code and domain‑specific program generation indicate verifier‑grounded repair can eliminate mechanically checkable errors when the verifier provides actionable diagnostics [2], [3].

Open questions remain about how GVR scales across heterogeneous template families, the concrete hosted‑LLM call cost per avoided violation, and how to interpret paired comparisons when initial candidate sampling is shared between conditions. To address these questions we preregistered and executed study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1, a paired, provenance‑traced confirmatory experiment in Mininet emulation. The study exercises three synthetic vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) under shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial sampled generation was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes, so any paired outcome difference could arise only from deterministic validation and permitted repair. We report the preregistered confirmatory test, exploratory interval estimates, audited provider accounting, and representative validator traces drawn directly from the archived execution and analysis bundles.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and NetOps‑specific reviews document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps and recurring evaluation gaps, notably benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. NetConfEval and related benchmark efforts examine LLMs for configuration tasks and expose common failure modes, but they typically lack provenance‑traced verifier pipelines spanning heterogeneous template families [4]. Adjacent domain work demonstrates that verifier‑grounded generate–verify‑repair patterns reduce mechanically checkable errors in code and domain programs when a deterministic verifier or oracle exists [2], [3].

Our study situates itself within this literature by (i) providing a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory evaluation across heterogeneous synthetic templates in a Mininet emulator, (ii) executing shared_initial_candidate semantics so that paired differences reflect only deterministic validator/repair effects, and (iii) reporting audited hosted‑model call accounting to quantify repair cost. We intentionally avoid production‑readiness claims and instead present an artifact‑grounded proof‑of‑concept under a tightly specified scope consistent with the prior literature's identified gaps.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The experiment was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50). The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded minus baseline) tested by an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Predeclared exploratory outputs include a paired bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and cost descriptors (mean extra hosted model calls per intent and per avoided violation).

Sampling, strata, and sampling semantics: N = 200 unique operator intents were deterministically selected and stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) as specified in the frozen task_index_profile. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initially sampled generation was produced and reused by both the baseline and guarded episodes. Under this semantics the baseline outcome equals the validator's verdict on that single shared candidate; the guarded outcome equals the final result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms or independent first‑pass resampling were not executed; therefore observed paired differences derive solely from the validator/repair pipeline and not from distinct initial draws.

Model configuration and temperature notation: The declared model in archived artifacts is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset. We state explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The execution budget constrained initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, with maximum_model_calls = 400.

Deterministic validator and repair policy: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements (a) syntactic parsing and canonicalization of configuration commands, (b) required‑command sequencing checks against per‑task required_sequence constraints, (c) emulation‑based reachability/topology verification against the provided initial network state, and (d) encoded ACL/policy checks expressed in the task payload. The validator yields a boolean success = "no detected violations" according to the predeclared full_intent_constraint_validation scoring rule. When the validator reports violations, the guarded pipeline may issue at most one repair call: the repair prompt is constructed deterministically from the validator's localized diagnostics (violating commands and the minimal corrective guidance required) and sent to the same declared hosted model. Repair calls were issued only when the validator returned violations; all validator traces (validation_before/validation_after) and repair decisions are archived and form the basis of contingency accounting.

Scoring, missingness, and confirmatory analysis plan: The preregistered primary test is exact McNemar two‑sided on paired binary success indicators. Exclusion rules predeclared deterministic duplicate detection and unrecoverable infrastructure failures as grounds for exclusion, with conservative sensitivity analyses treating ambiguous verifier outputs as violations. In execution no pairs were excluded or failed. The bootstrap CI and cost descriptors are exploratory and reported with explicit caution regarding small discordant counts, as described below.

Deterministic provider accounting and auditability: The execution_manifest and deterministic_reconciliation record hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls; cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 204. Stage accounting reports shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair stage = 4. These audited counts are reported verbatim in Results to permit independent reconciliation with archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and paired outcomes: The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; failed_episode_count = 0. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory inference and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; the null is not rejected at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]; the bootstrap seed and resampling count are recorded in analysis_log.jsonl. We caution that when discordant pair counts (n10 + n01) are small, bootstrap percentile intervals can be unstable; therefore the McNemar exact p‑value is the preregistered formal test and the bootstrap interval is presented for descriptive magnitude context only.

Repair incidence and hosted‑call cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across 200 intents. Total hosted model calls = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs), yielding mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent due to repairs = 0.02. Each repair corrected one baseline failure in the archived contingency table, giving mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. These arithmetic derivations follow directly from the audited provider_call counts in deterministic_reconciliation and execution_manifest and are reported verbatim.

Representative validator traces and discordant‑pair anatomy: Representative execution/scoring task artifacts (e.g., task‑000004, task‑000005, task‑000006 entries in execution/scoring/) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and identical shared_initial response text used by both baseline and guarded episodes, confirming shared_initial_candidate semantics in practice. For each discordant pair the archived validator_trace.validation_before recorded one or more violating elements (e.g., missing required sequencing or topology contradictions) and validator_trace.validation_after recorded that a repair was applied (repair_applied = true) and the final configuration passed full_intent_constraint_validation. The per‑episode artifacts substantiate the contingency counts and the repair accounting above.

Statistical diagnostics and power context: The preregistered power plan targeted detection of a 10 percentage‑point absolute reduction with n ≈ 157 (McNemar approximation) and selected N = 200 to allow stratified description. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) was smaller than some planning scenarios, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements and producing the small discordant count observed (n10 + n01 = 4). This explains the non‑significant McNemar result despite a positive point estimate and underscores the importance of planning under realistic baseline rates for confirmatory designs.

Exploratory subgroup summaries (descriptive): The preregistration stratified tasks across three vendor template families and four topology patterns; execution manifest confirms that sampling and stratification were deterministic. The archived artifacts contain per‑task difficulty metadata (difficulty.level and required_command_count) and per‑episode validator difficulty summaries that can support detailed subgroup description. Because the preregistered primary test is global and confirmatory, per‑stratum descriptions are reported as exploratory in the archived analysis artifacts rather than as additional confirmatory claims in this paper.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics: By design and per the preregistration, shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed: a single sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused across baseline and guarded episodes. Therefore paired improvements derive only from deterministic validator/repair actions and not from independent first‑pass re‑sampling or prompt engineering. This design isolates verifier/repair effects but does not measure how alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample generation would affect first‑pass validity.

Construct validity and residual semantic risk: The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 covers syntactic, sequencing, topology/reachability, and encoded ACL/policy checks as expressible in per‑task constraints; it cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations that are not formalized in its rule set. Consequently, the observed elimination of mechanically detectable baseline violations by guarded repairs does not imply elimination of all semantic errors. Extending verifier coverage to formalize additional semantic/policy ontologies is a high‑priority direction to reduce residual false negatives.

Internal validity, nondeterminism, and temperature reporting: The archived model_configuration.json declares requested_model = gpt‑5‑mini and records temperature = null/unset. We emphasize that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The deterministic_reconciliation and provider_call_audit show hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 with no failed calls; cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 204 indicate each call was executed against the hosted provider. These audited counts permit independent reconciliation with raw provider traces in the archived bundle.

Operational implications and bounded claims: In this template‑driven Mininet emulation a small repair budget (four repairs) removed the mechanically detectable baseline violations at low hosted‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02). This artifact‑grounded observation suggests that, when a verifier can express and check the relevant constraints and supply localized diagnostics, bounded repair budgets can be effective in removing mechanically checkable faults in comparable emulated, template‑driven settings. We do not claim generalization to production hardware, different prompt families, other LLMs, or to semantic errors outside the verifier's coverage.

Reproducibility, archival assets, and recommended next steps: All execution and analysis artifacts described here are archived in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration and execution manifests, enabling independent verification of counts, paired tables, validator traces, and provider accounting. Recommended next steps grounded in archived evidence: (1) widen deterministic verifier coverage to encode more semantic/policy checks and measure residual false negatives; (2) perform paired designs with independent multi‑sample initial generations to separate prompt/template effects from validator effects; (3) evaluate multiple hosted models and versions to quantify sensitivity to provider nondeterminism and model updates; (4) preserve provenance tracing and deterministic hashing for all provider calls and validator traces to enable forensic reconciliation. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifact evidence and stated limitations.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator; future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

Preregistration: C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 (SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50) was recorded before any model calls. Sampling semantics: execution used shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded); archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset (null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). Provider accounting (audited): hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial generations + 4 repair calls. Reported numbers and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundles.
limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
